email.subject: URGENT: Your account will be suspended in 24 hours
email.body: Dear valued customer, we noticed unusual sign-in activity on your profile. URGENT: Your account will be suspended in 24 hours unless you confirm your details right now.

redFlags.explanation: Watch out for lookalike brand spelling and extra hyphenated domains. Official companies rarely email security alerts from third-party addresses.

redFlags.text: URGENT: Your account will be suspended in 24 hours
redFlags.explanation: Panic-inducing deadlines are classic bait to rush you into clicking before thinking. Slow down and check your real account page directly.
Generic greetings show the message was blasted to thousands of people at once. Real service emails usually know your actual name.

fieldGuide.howItWorks: Scammers cast a wide net by sending the exact same fake alert to millions of addresses, hoping a small fraction panic and hand over login credentials.
howToSpot: Look closely at the sender address for misspelled brands or odd domains.
Spot manufactured countdowns or threats of sudden account deletion.
Notice vague greetings like 'Dear valued customer' instead of your name.
fieldGuide.whatToDo: Ignore the email link and open the official website or app yourself to check if there is any real notice.

email.subject: Updated Q4 bonus sheet for Maya
email.body: Hi Maya, I put together the updated Q4 bonus sheet for Maya ahead of today's review. Please review the attached spreadsheet before noon and sign off.

redFlags.explanation: A familiar-looking name paired with a slightly off domain is a big clue. Always double-check the exact domain after the @ symbol.
Unexpected spreadsheets or 'urgent review' files can hide malicious macros or fake login forms. Confirm with the sender over a trusted channel first.
Tight same-day cutoffs pressure you into opening files fast. Legitimate teammates won't mind a quick verification call or chat message.

fieldGuide.howItWorks: Unlike mass blasts, spear phishing tailors the message with personal or workplace details so it feels familiar and trustworthy at first glance.
howToSpot: Verify the sender's full email domain even when the display name looks familiar.
Be cautious of unexpected spreadsheets, invoices, or review links.
Watch for tight deadlines paired with requests to open files or log in.
fieldGuide.whatToDo: Message or call the person using a known contact method to confirm they actually sent the file or request.

email.subject: Keep this quiet — confidential wire needed
email.body: Keep this quiet — confidential wire needed while I am in back-to-back board meetings. Send an immediate transfer to settle this vendor matter discreetly.

redFlags.explanation: An executive claiming to be on company business from a free webmail address is a classic red flag. Check the official company domain.
Requests for fast money transfers or gift cards via email should always trigger extra care. Follow standard approval steps no matter who asks.

redFlags.text: Keep this quiet — confidential wire needed
redFlags.explanation: Asking you to keep a financial request secret stops you from getting a second pair of eyes. Real finance workflows don't rely on secrecy.

fieldGuide.howItWorks: Big-fish attackers impersonate executives or directors and ask employees to move money or share sensitive data quickly and quietly.
howToSpot: Check if a leader is emailing from an unverified or personal address.
Spot demands for secrecy, discretion, or skipping normal approval steps.
Be alert to urgent payment, wire, or gift card requests.
fieldGuide.whatToDo: Pause any payment and verify the request directly through your finance team or established out-of-band channels.

email.subject: Re: Shared folder 'Team_Designs_Final' — new version
email.body: Here is the revised copy of the message you saw earlier with an updated link. Re: Shared folder 'Team_Designs_Final' — new version is ready to view.

redFlags.explanation: Even when the wording mirrors a real notice, the sender domain is a lookalike. Always check where the email actually came from.
A 'revised' link inside a cloned message often points to a credential-stealing page. Navigate to your real cloud storage instead of clicking.

redFlags.text: Here is the revised copy of the message you saw earlier with an updated link
redFlags.explanation: Claiming to resend an earlier message with a 'new link' is a common trick to swap in a malicious URL. Compare it with your original thread.

fieldGuide.howItWorks: Attackers copy a legitimate or previously seen email and swap out the link or attachment for a harmful version while keeping the text familiar.
howToSpot: Compare the sender address against genuine emails from the same service.
Watch for 'updated link' or 'revised version' claims out of nowhere.
Hover or inspect link destinations before opening shared files.
fieldGuide.whatToDo: Open your cloud drive or service directly in a new tab and locate the file without using the email's link.

email.subject: Invoice #INV-88412 overdue — automatic charge failed
email.body: Your card was declined for Invoice #INV-88412 overdue — automatic charge failed. Download the itemized bill and update your payment card today.

redFlags.explanation: Billing scams love tacking words like '-invoices' onto a brand name. Check your real account portal to see if an invoice actually exists.
Fake 'invoice PDF' buttons can lead to spoofed payment pages or unwanted downloads. Never enter card details from an email link.
A sudden 'failed charge' notice tries to make you re-enter your card number in a hurry. Log in through your saved bookmark to check billing.

fieldGuide.howItWorks: Slippery billing lures send fake overdue notices or failed payment alerts so victims hand over credit card numbers or open booby-trapped files.
howToSpot: Check if you recognize the subscription, order, or invoice number.
Look out for extra words added to a company's domain name.
Avoid entering payment card details through links inside billing emails.
fieldGuide.whatToDo: Log in to your account directly from a trusted bookmark or app to check your real billing status.

email.subject: Parcel delivery failed: pay $2.99 re-delivery fee
email.body: We tried to deliver your package today, but Parcel delivery failed: pay $2.99 re-delivery fee so your courier can reschedule drop-off.

redFlags.explanation: Couriers rarely send payment links from '-redelivery.info' addresses. Check the tracking number on the official carrier site.
Small 'redelivery' fees are a classic trap to steal card numbers and billing addresses. Treat surprise fee prompts with suspicion.
Clicking a payment button in a surprise delivery text or email can send you straight to a fake checkout page. Verify your order first.

fieldGuide.howItWorks: Delivery darts strike when people are expecting packages, using a tiny fee or missed-delivery alert to capture card details.
howToSpot: Question any surprise fee—even a tiny one—for missed delivery.
Inspect the sender domain for unofficial add-ons like '-redelivery'.
Check whether you actually ordered anything with a matching tracking ID.
fieldGuide.whatToDo: Go straight to the carrier's or store's official website and track your package there instead of paying through the email.

email.subject: Unrecognized browser sign-in blocked
email.body: Someone attempted to sign in from a new device. Unrecognized browser sign-in blocked — sign in here to review your session settings.

redFlags.explanation: Notice the misspelled brand name and extra security words in the domain. That address isn't the real company.
Links telling you to 'sign in here' from an email are a prime way attackers harvest passwords. Always type or bookmark the real sign-in page.
A scary security alert nudges you to type your password without checking the web address. Stay calm and open your account directly.

fieldGuide.howItWorks: Fake login rays lure you to a lookalike sign-in page designed to copy your username, password, and sometimes your one-time login code.
howToSpot: Spot subtle misspellings in the brand name or sender domain.
Be wary of emails asking you to log in via an embedded button.
Check the browser address bar before ever typing a password.
fieldGuide.whatToDo: Close the email, open the site yourself via a trusted bookmark or app, and check your active sessions there.

email.subject: Mailbox 99% full — mailbox deletion warning
email.body: Your storage quota is almost reached. Mailbox 99% full — mailbox deletion warning will apply unless you validate your webmail credentials.

redFlags.explanation: Generic 'IT Helpdesk' names paired with outside or lookalike domains are a classic trap. Verify the sender address carefully.
Threatening to wipe your inbox over storage quota is a pressure tactic to steal your login. Real quota notices don't demand password entry via email links.
No legitimate support desk needs you to 'validate your credentials' through a random link. Report suspicious IT emails to your real security team.

fieldGuide.howItWorks: Scammers pose as IT support or helpdesk staff, claiming your mailbox or account is about to be deleted so you hand over your login.
howToSpot: Watch for alarming warnings about mailbox deletion or quota expiration.
Check if the sender address matches your actual organization or provider.
Be suspicious of any prompt to re-enter or 'validate' account passwords.
fieldGuide.whatToDo: Don't enter your password on linked pages—check your storage in account settings or contact your real IT team.
